blocks.h2: How a Tankless Water Heater Works
blocks.body: Instead of keeping a tank of water hot all day, a tankless heater fires only when a hot tap opens. Water flows through a heat exchanger and comes out hot for as long as you need it. The limit is flow rate: a unit can only heat so many gallons per minute, so it has to be sized for your busiest moment, like a shower running while the washer fills.

blocks.h2: Is Tankless Right for Your Skokie Home?
blocks.intro: Many Skokie homes can switch, but a few things need checking first.

items.body: Postwar gas lines were sized for a furnace and a tank heater. A tankless unit may need a larger line.
Tankless units can't use the old chimney. They vent through the wall or roof.
Freeing up floor space is a plus in compact basements.
Even Lake Michigan water leaves minerals in the heat exchanger over time.

blocks.h2: Does Tankless Fit a Skokie Ranch?
blocks.body: In a ranch or Cape Cod with a basement utility area, a wall-mounted tankless heater can open up floor space for storage or laundry. The vent usually runs out through the rim joist to the side yard. The gas line from the meter may need to be larger. We look at both before quoting, so you know the full scope of the job.

items.q: Can a tankless heater use my existing chimney?
items.preview: No. It needs its own vent.
items.answer: No. Tankless units vent through their own pipe, usually through a side wall.

items.q: Will my gas line need to be replaced?
items.preview: Often it needs to be upsized.
items.answer: Often. Many postwar gas lines are too small for a tankless unit. We check before we quote.

items.q: How often should a tankless unit be descaled?
items.answer: About once a year for most homes.
Yes. We diagnose error codes, descale heat exchangers, clean sensors and replace failed parts.

items.q: Is tankless worth it for two people?
items.answer: Sometimes. Smaller households save less, but gain space and endless hot water.
